opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core of it was that we had a number of really strong teams, in Google Brain, in DeepMind, and elsewhere in Google Research, who were all working on large language models and multimodal models, and they were doing really good work. But each effort was pursuing a somewhat similar goal with its own slice of the compute, its own data pipelines, its own infrastructure, and its own set of very talented people.

When you're training models at the scale that matters now, that fragmentation gets expensive. You're essentially splitting your compute across several efforts, and none of them gets enough to train the best model you could build if you pooled everything. So I wrote a fairly short memo internally saying, look, we're being kind of silly here. We should combine our compute, combine our people, and try to train one really excellent multimodal model, rather than three or four that are each pretty good.

The other part was that the ideas from these groups were complementary. DeepMind had deep expertise in reinforcement learning and some very strong modeling work. Brain had a lot of the Transformer lineage, the infrastructure work with TPUs, and experience scaling things up. Bringing those together meant we could take the best ideas from each and not just the best hardware allocation.

We also wanted it to be multimodal from the start. We didn't want a text model with vision bolted on later. The world isn't just text. It's images, video, audio, and code. Building that in from the beginning is a big undertaking, and it's much more realistic as one coordinated effort than as several smaller ones.

Of course, combining teams that large comes with real challenges. People are spread across many time zones and have different cultures and ways of working. But I think it has worked out well. Having one shared model effort that everyone contributes to, and that then gets used across many Google products, has been a much better outcome than what we had before.

r001.rationale: The response says talented people were split across separate efforts and recommends combining them into one effort.

r002.rationale: It says the groups had complementary ideas and that combining them would bring together the best ideas from each.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says, “We also wanted it to be multimodal from the start.”

fable-5.1.text:
So the context was that by late 2022, early 2023, we had Google Brain and we had DeepMind, and both groups were building large language models. Brain had PaLM and the models that came after it, DeepMind had Chinchilla and Gopher and that line of work. And these were really good teams, doing really good work, but they were somewhat duplicative. We were both building the same kinds of distributed training infrastructure, both doing data curation, both doing scaling studies, and so on.

And at the same time, it was becoming pretty clear that the frontier of what you could do with these models was moving to larger and larger scale. The compute requirements were going up a lot. So if you had two separate efforts, each one would get maybe half the compute, half the data work, half the engineering attention, and you'd end up with two models that were both not as good as the one model you could have built if you'd pooled everything together.

The other thing is that these models are really multidisciplinary. You need people who are great at systems and compilers and getting the most out of the TPUs. You need people who are great at the pretraining recipe, people who are great at post-training and RL, people who are great at evaluation, at safety, at multimodal work. And both Brain and DeepMind had strengths in different pieces of that. DeepMind had a lot of depth in reinforcement learning, Brain had a lot of depth in the systems side and in things like multimodal. So putting them together actually gave you a more complete team, not just a bigger one.

So I think the argument was fairly straightforward: this is the most important thing the company can be working on, it's really expensive to do well, and you don't want to be competing with yourself for the same resources. It was better to have one really ambitious effort where everyone was pulling in the same direction. That's what became Gemini, and I think the results bear that out. It wasn't painless, there's a lot of work in merging two cultures and two codebases, but I think it was the right call.

r001.rationale: The response says Brain and DeepMind had separate teams with complementary strengths, and that combining them pooled expertise into a more complete team.

r002.rationale: It describes duplicated work and complementary team strengths, but does not clearly say that the best ideas were fragmented across the efforts.

r003.rationale: It mentions multimodal work as one needed specialty and a Brain strength, but does not state that Gemini was intended to be multimodal from the outset.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think we had a lot of really talented people working on somewhat overlapping efforts in Google Brain and DeepMind. And it seemed like we could accomplish more by bringing those people together around one ambitious effort, rather than having multiple teams independently trying to build the best foundational model.

These models require a pretty substantial investment in compute, but also a very broad range of expertise—in algorithms, data, infrastructure, and how you actually make the models useful. Bringing that expertise together lets you combine the best ideas and put more of our resources behind a shared direction.

And we wanted that direction to be multimodal from the beginning. Language is important, but we also want models that can understand images, audio, video, and code. Gemini was an opportunity to bring those capabilities together with a team that could really pursue that ambition.

r001.rationale: It says talented people were spread across overlapping Brain and DeepMind efforts and that bringing them together would help the teams accomplish more.

r002.rationale: It says bringing the teams’ expertise together would let them combine the best ideas around a shared direction.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says Gemini’s direction was to be multimodal from the beginning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic motivation was that we had a lot of talented people working on related problems in different parts of Google. There’s value in exploring different approaches, but training these large models also requires a substantial investment in compute, data, and engineering. It made sense to bring those efforts together so we could build on one another’s ideas and put more of our resources behind a really strong model.

And we wanted something that was multimodal from the start—that could work with language, images, audio, and video. That’s a broad research and engineering challenge, and bringing the teams together gave us a better way to tackle it.

r001.rationale: It says talented people worked on related problems in different parts of Google, but does not identify them as Google’s best researchers.

r002.rationale: It says the teams could build on one another’s ideas, but does not clearly state that Google’s best ideas were fragmented across separate efforts.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says Gemini should be multimodal “from the start,” and names language, images, audio, and video.
